name: MIMA
overview: Middlesbrough Institute of Modern Art, an art gallery on Centre Square in central Middlesbrough (Wikipedia).
Formally launched on 27 January 2007, after construction began in 2004. Its first director, Godfrey Worsdale, left in 2008 for the Baltic Centre for Contemporary Art (Wikipedia).
The building was designed by Erick van Egeraat Associated Architects and cost £14.2 million (Attractions Management, 31 January 2007).
funding_verdict: MIMA: mainly public: Arts Council England and Middlesbrough Council, through Teesside University

name: 78 Derngate
overview: House museum and visitor centre on Derngate in Northampton, run by The 78 Derngate Northampton Trust, a charitable company limited by guarantee (accounts).

The Trust was formed in 1998 after Northampton Borough Council bought a 999-year lease on 78 and 80 Derngate in 1996. The house opened to the public in late 2003 (the house's site, English Wikipedia).
Named for its street number. The house is also called The Charles Rennie Mackintosh House (the house's site).
funding_verdict: 78 Derngate: donation-led charity, built with lottery and local-authority money

name: Newlyn Art Gallery
overview: Contemporary art gallery in Newlyn, Cornwall, with a second venue, The Exchange, in Penzance. The two are about 2 km apart, a 20 to 30 minute walk along the seafront (gallery visit page).

Opened in 1895 with the Le Grice family giving the land and the philanthropist John Passmore Edwards supporting it (gallery website). Wikipedia adds that it was designed by James Hicks of Redruth and was conceived as a home and exhibition venue for the Newlyn School of Art.
In 2007 it redeveloped the Newlyn site, after a RIBA design competition, and took over Penzance's former telephone exchange as The Exchange (gallery website, Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Newlyn Art Gallery: mainly public: Arts Council England and Cornwall Council, plus trusts and earned income
wider_context: On 29 May 2026 The New Arab (staff report) described an open letter signed by more than 260 British artists and published by Artists for Palestine UK, urging the National Theatre, Royal Shakespeare Company, Young Vic, Royal Court and Almeida to end partnerships with Bloomberg Philanthropies. The letter calls the organisation "complicit in grave war crimes" against Palestinians and cites the Bloomberg-Sagol Center at Tel Aviv University.
The same report says Bloomberg's Regional Recovery and Repair Initiative contributed up to 27.8 million dollars to Israeli communities affected by the war in Gaza.
The connection to the gallery: the gallery says it joined the Bloomberg Philanthropies Digital Accelerator programme in 2025. The letter names five London theatres, not Newlyn.

name: Bloc Projects
overview: Artist-led contemporary art space at 71 Eyre Lane, Sheffield S1 4RB, supporting the professional development of artists. It describes its programme as "radical, ambitious, socially relevant and critically engaged art practices" (Bloc Projects website).

Founded in 2002 by a group of artists at Bloc Studios (Bloc Projects website). Richard Bartle founded Bloc Studios on Sidney Street. The gallery began as an informal, volunteer-run project space inside the studios and became a formal gallery in 2007 (Now Then, 2015 interview).
Corridor8 marked its tenth anniversary in 2012, describing it as open to artists "at a point of change or risk in their career" (Robert Clark).
funding_verdict: Bloc Projects: small artist-led registered charity: government grants and a National Lottery Heritage Fund award

name: Yorkshire Sculpture Park
overview: Open-air sculpture park of about 500 acres in the grounds of Bretton Hall, an 18th-century estate at West Bretton, Wakefield, West Yorkshire (Wikipedia).
Founded by Peter Murray and opened in 1977. Wikipedia calls it the UK's first sculpture park.
The hall was a family home until the mid-20th century and then became Bretton Hall College (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Yorkshire Sculpture Park: public and private mix: Arts Council England, Wakefield Council, the Bramall Foundation, the Dunard Fund, Roger Evans, individuals and corporate partners

name: Cranbrook Art Museum
overview: Art museum of the Cranbrook Educational Community, a National Historic Landmark District in Bloomfield Hills, Michigan, at 39221 Woodward Avenue (Wikipedia; Cranbrook).

The Cranbrook estate began as a 174-acre farm bought in 1904. Cranbrook Academy of Art was founded in 1932 and the museum building was completed in 1942 under the architect Eliel Saarinen. It closed for renovation in 2009 and reopened in November 2011 (Wikipedia).

Visiting: open Wednesday to Sunday 11am to 5pm, Thursday until 8pm, closed Monday and Tuesday. Admission $12, seniors and Detroit residents $10, students $8, children 12 and under, ArtMembers and EBT or WIC cardholders free, and Thursdays free. Barrier-free access at the front turnaround and the New Studios Building. Free parking.
funding_verdict: Cranbrook Art Museum: private: foundations, a corporate sponsor and members, inside the Cranbrook Educational Community

press_items.title: Maya Pontone, "Students Protest After Michigan Art School Takes Down Palestinian Flags" (2023)

name: The Renaissance Society
overview: Free, independent, non-collecting contemporary art museum on the University of Chicago campus, in Cobb Hall, 4th floor, 5811 South Ellis Avenue (Wikipedia; museum site). It presents about four exhibitions a year, plus concerts, lectures and screenings.

Founded in 1915, in the wake of the 1913 Armory Show. Ten University of Chicago professors convened the first exploratory meeting on 20 April 1915. Its constitution provides that all acquisitions except money become the property of the University of Chicago (Wikipedia).
Directors: Susanne Ghez led it from 1974 to 2013 (Wikipedia; the museum site gives 1973), Solveig Øvstebø from 2013, and Myriam Ben Salah has been executive director and chief curator since 2020.
funding_verdict: The Renaissance Society: foundation-funded: Mellon, Teiger and Warhol foundations and Chicago family foundations, with the University of Chicago about 5 percent

name: Magazzino Italian Art
overview: Museum and research center for postwar and contemporary Italian art at 2700 Route 9, Cold Spring, New York, in the Hudson Valley (museum website), about 80 km north of New York (Artribune).

Founded by the married collectors Nancy Olnick and Giorgio Spanu. Inaugurated in June 2017 with the exhibition "Rebel with a cause" (museum website). Wikipedia gives the public opening as 28 June 2017.
"Magazzino" is Italian for "warehouse." Wikipedia says the building was a computer chip factory. The Art Newspaper (2017) calls it a former dairy distribution centre.
funding_verdict: Magazzino Italian Art: self-funded: the founders' own money and gifts to a foundation they control

name: Crow Museum of Asian Art
aliases: Trammell and Margaret Crow Museum of Asian Art
Trammell and Margaret Crow Collection of Asian Art
overview: Museum of Asian art run by The University of Texas at Dallas, with its original building at 2010 Flora Street in the Dallas Arts District and a second site in the university's Edith and Peter O'Donnell Jr. Athenaeum (museum website).
Trammell and Margaret Crow bought their first piece of Asian art in the mid-1960s and opened the Trammell and Margaret Crow Collection of Asian Art as a free museum in December 1998 (museum website).

Collection: art from China, Japan, India, Korea and Southeast Asia, bought mostly from dealers, auction houses and whole collections such as Morrie A. Moss's; the Asian art expert Clarence Shangraw chose 569 pieces for the permanent collection (museum website). The 2019 gift counted more than 1,000 works (UT Dallas, 24 January 2019).
funding_verdict: Crow Museum of Asian Art: family gift to a state university: the Crow family, the O'Donnell Foundation and UT Dallas

name: Nasher Sculpture Center
overview: Sculpture museum and garden at 2001 Flora Street in the Dallas Arts District, across from the Dallas Museum of Art (Wikipedia, the museum's own site).
Founded from the collection of Raymond and Patsy Nasher, who began collecting sculpture in the 1950s. Raymond Nasher bought the land in 1997 and the Center opened in 2003 (Wikipedia).
Named for the Nasher family. The museum also awards the Nasher Prize, established in April 2015 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Nasher Sculpture Center: built with the Nasher Foundation's $70 million; contributions were 99.8% of revenue in the year to June 2025
wider_context: Hyperallergic (Samuel Rowlett, "How to Destroy a James Turrell", 18 June 2013) criticises Museum Tower, a 40-story condominium in the Dallas Arts District: Turrell declared Tending (Blue) destroyed because the tower blocks the sky view from the skyspace, and the tower's reflected light affects the Nasher's gallery conditions, keeps works on paper from being shown and harms trees in the Peter Walker garden.

Unverified: Raymond Nasher had a "gentleman's agreement" with the Dallas Police and Fire Pension System, whose real estate arm wanted to build the tower, to keep it under 20 stories, and the design changed after he died in 2007, from an insider account that Rowlett relays and does not confirm.
The article criticises the tower's developer, not the Nasher.

name: Fay and Gus Jones House
overview: Architect's own house at 1330 N. Hillcrest Avenue in Fayetteville, Arkansas, on a lot beside a wooded area at the northern edge of town (Encyclopedia of Arkansas, fayjoneshouse.com).
Fay Jones designed it in 1956 as his family home and it was completed in May 1956. Fay Jones died in 2004 and Gus Jones in 2014 (fayjoneshouse.com, Encyclopedia of Arkansas).
Named for Fay and Gus Jones, who built it as their family home. No earlier name found (fayjoneshouse.com, Encyclopedia of Arkansas).
funding_verdict: Fay and Gus Jones House: university-owned: a public university, a state council grant and private donors

name: Takaezu Studio
overview: Working pottery studio in the former home and studio of the ceramist Toshiko Takaezu at 1177 Croton Road, Flemington, New Jersey. She lived and worked in Quakertown for over 30 years and taught at Princeton University (studio site).
Takaezu (1922 to 2011) established a permanent studio and house in Quakertown in 1975 (English Wikipedia), the year she began a live-in apprenticeship there (Clay Art Center).

Named for Takaezu. After her death Donald Fletcher and his wife bought the place and live there, according to a 2019 JerseyArts.com article by Susan Wallner, which says the studio now runs as a foundation with exhibition space and a residency programme.
funding_verdict: Takaezu Studio: privately funded: gifts to Quakertown Studio Project from donors the public summaries do not name

name: Liljestrand House
overview: House museum at 3300 Tantalus Drive on Mount Tantalus above Honolulu, about 15 minutes by car from downtown and 30 minutes from Waikiki. The upstairs lanai looks onto Lē‘ahi (Diamond Head) (liljestrandhouse.org).

Vladimir Ossipoff designed it in 1948 for Dr. Howard and Betty Liljestrand and it was built in 1952 for $40,000 (Associated Press). It is named for the family. Howard Liljestrand died in 2004 and his four children inherited it. They created the Liljestrand Foundation in 2007 and ownership passed to the Foundation in December 2015 (liljestrandhouse.org).

Wood frame with concrete block retaining walls, bleach-stained redwood interiors and a sandstone fireplace, on about one acre. Listed on the National Register on 26 March 2008 (English Wikipedia). Kitty Thompson is credited with the original grounds, which the Foundation is reviewing for selective restoration (liljestrandhouse.org).
funding_verdict: Liljestrand House: private non-profit: family foundation living on donations and tour and program income, with no endowment

name: The Frank Lloyd Wright House in Ebsworth Park
overview: Frank Lloyd Wright's Kraus House at 120 North Ballas Road, Kirkwood, Missouri, with a St. Louis mailing address, in a 10.5-acre park (Ebsworth Park, English Wikipedia).
Wright designed it in 1950 for Russell and Ruth Kraus, who moved in during January 1956 (Ebsworth Park). The Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation gives 1951 as the build year and Iconic Houses gives 1958.
Named for the Kraus family. The nonprofit calls it The Frank Lloyd Wright House in Ebsworth Park, and no page read explains the name Ebsworth.
funding_verdict: The Frank Lloyd Wright House in Ebsworth Park: private nonprofit: gifts and tours, with St. Louis County as title holder

name: Laguna Art Museum
overview: Laguna Art Museum, 307 Cliff Dr., Laguna Beach (museum website).
Founded by local artists in 1918 (museum website, About page).

What is there: a permanent collection of California-based work spanning 1860 to the present, with emphasis on key California artists, especially works made since 2000, and on equal representation of women; built almost entirely through gifts from artists, galleries and individuals. The page gives no total count (museum website, Collection page).
funding_verdict: Laguna Art Museum: private gifts, with a bank and a foundation named as supporters

name: Frelinghuysen Morris House & Studio
overview: House museum at 92 Hawthorne Street on a 46-acre estate that borders Tanglewood, a 10-minute woodland walk from the parking area (the house's site).

Suzy Frelinghuysen left instructions at her death in 1988 that the house and collection be used for an educational purpose, her co-trustees set up a charitable foundation, and it opened to visitors in July 1998 after Lenox and Stockbridge approved it (the house's site, Berkshire Eagle 2018).
Named for the two abstract artists who lived there, George L. K. Morris and Suzy Frelinghuysen.
funding_verdict: Frelinghuysen Morris House & Studio: endowed: Suzy Frelinghuysen's bequest, with income from investments

name: Coaxial Arts Foundation
overview: Artist-run non-profit art space in a storefront at 1815 South Main Street in downtown Los Angeles, dedicated to experimental video, sound and performance art (Matt Stromberg, Hyperallergic, 27 March 2019; Coaxial website).
Founded by Eva Aguila. Her partner Brock Fansler is its treasurer (Joshua Oduga, "A Los Angeles Residency Envisions a Radical Future for Experimental Art", Hyperallergic, 26 March 2024).

Hyperallergic (2024) says the residency launched in 2016 with inaugural residents JJ Stratford and Suzy Poling, and that residents work without curator oversight and receive studio space and access to video and sound equipment. The Coaxial website says it has run residencies since March 2015.
funding_verdict: Coaxial Arts Foundation: grant-funded and earned income: public arts agencies, private foundations and ticket and admission income

name: Human Resources LA (HRLA)
overview: Volunteer-run non-profit exhibition and performance space at 410 Cottage Home Street, Chinatown, Los Angeles (Human Resources website).
Founded in 2010 by siblings Eric and Kathleen Kim with Giles Miller, Devin McNulty and Dawn Kasper, who wanted to put performance art ahead of static displays (Wikipedia).
The name presents the space as a resource for artists rather than an institution (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Human Resources LA: grant-funded non-profit: arts foundations and a county arts commission, with individual contributions

name: Frank Lloyd Wright Houses at the Currier Museum
overview: Two Usonian houses by Frank Lloyd Wright, the Zimmerman House at 223 Heather Street in Manchester's North End and the Kalil House on the same street, shown on guided tours run by the Currier Museum of Art at 150 Ash Street (currier.org, English Wikipedia).

Isadore and Lucille Zimmerman commissioned their house in 1949. They left it to the museum in 1988 and it opened to the public in 1990. Wright designed the Kalil House in 1955 for Toufic and Mildred Kalil, who were inspired by their neighbours the Zimmermans, and the museum bought it in 2019 (currier.org, English Wikipedia).
Named for the first clients. The Zimmerman House is also catalogued as the Isadore J. and Lucille Zimmerman House (English Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Currier Museum of Art: private non-profit museum: endowment, donors and tickets, with a named corporate sponsor roster

name: Ballroom Marfa
overview: Non-collecting contemporary art museum at 108 E. San Antonio Street in Marfa, Texas, a town of fewer than 2,000 people in Far West Texas (museum site).

Established in 2003 by Virginia Lebermann and Fairfax Dorn. Lebermann is president of the board and Dorn artistic director (museum site). ProPublica's Form 990 data lists Daisy Nam as executive director.
Housed in a 1920s-era ballroom at 108 E. San Antonio Street (museum site).
funding_verdict: Ballroom Marfa: philanthropic: individuals and foundations, with small public grants
wider_context: Hyperallergic (Laura C. Mallonee, "Marfa's Art World Gentrification Is Pushing Out Long-Time Residents", 11 August 2014): a reappraisal of Presidio County properties found values roughly doubled in a year, from $563 million in 2013 to $1.14 billion, and residents protested. The article does not name Ballroom Marfa.

Ballroom's own Prada Marfa history page calls Elmgreen and Dragset's 2001 precursor to the piece "a playful commentary on how art galleries have contributed to the process of gentrification in urban areas". Ballroom is part of the Marfa art economy these pieces discuss.
